(1) Priya and Soraya have volunteered at the downtown food bank every Saturday since last winter. (2) They always start by sorting canned goods and checking expiration dates before the doors open. (3) Afterward, she restocks the shelves in the pantry while keeping a tally of what's running low. (4) Both girls hope to recruit more volunteers before the holiday season arrives.

Which sentence of the paragraph should be revised to correct a vague pronoun?

solution.exhibit_text:
Sentence 3 uses “she” (“she restocks the shelves”), but with two girls named in sentence 1 — Priya and Soraya — there's no way to tell which one “she” means.

If a sentence has two or more people or things it could plausibly point to — or if it doesn't clearly point to anything — the pronoun is vague. Fix it by swapping the pronoun back out for the actual name or noun, or by rewriting the sentence so only one candidate is possible.

grammar_questions.question:
(1) Wren, Omar, and Talia make fruit smoothies together every weekend at Wren's house. (2) Omar picks out ripe bananas and strawberries and drops them straight into the blender. (3) Wren adds a scoop of yogurt to each cup before they finish blending it into a thick creamy drink. (4) Talia pours the finished smoothies into three tall glasses for everyone to enjoy.

Which pair of revisions is needed to correct the errors in the paragraph?

options.A: Sentence 1: Delete the comma after **Omar**, AND change **make** to **makes**.
options.B: Sentence 2: Insert a comma after **bananas**, AND change **drops** to **drop**.

options.D: Sentence 4: Insert a comma after **tall**, AND change **pours** to **pour**.

solution.exhibit_text:
In sentence 3, “each cup” is singular, so the pronoun has to be singular too — “they finish” should be “it finishes.” A comma is also needed between “thick” and “creamy,” which both independently describe “drink” (you could just as easily say “creamy, thick drink”).

**The concept:** A pronoun has to match the number of the noun it's replacing — singular noun, singular pronoun ("it"); plural noun, plural pronoun ("they"/"them"). **The concept:** When two adjectives both independently describe the same noun (you could say them in either order, or put "and" between them — "calm and patient," "patient and calm"), they need a comma between them. grammar_questions.question:
Read these sentences.

(1) Weather balloon launches near the coast have been conducted since 1965. (2) Weather balloon launches allow scientists to collect data about upper-atmosphere wind patterns.

What is the **best** way to combine the sentences to clarify the relationship between the ideas?

options.A: While weather balloon launches near the coast have been conducted since 1965, scientists collect data about upper-atmosphere wind patterns.
options.B: Although there have been weather balloon launches near the coast since 1965, they have allowed scientists to collect data about upper-atmosphere wind patterns.
options.C: Weather balloon launches near the coast, which allow scientists to collect data about upper-atmosphere wind patterns, have been conducted since 1965.
options.D: Weather balloon launches have been conducted near the coast, but scientists have been collecting data about upper-atmosphere wind patterns since 1965.

solution.exhibit_text:
(C) nests the purpose of the launches — collecting wind-pattern data — in a nonrestrictive “which” clause, keeping the main point (that the launches have been happening since 1965) as the main clause. “While,” “although,” and “but” all wrongly suggest contrast or coincidence instead of purpose.

**The concept:** When combining several short sentences about one subject, there's usually one "main point" and the rest are supporting details. The strongest combination makes the main point the main clause and folds the other facts in as describing phrases or clauses, in whatever order makes the most logical sense. Watch out for answers that just string everything together with "and," since that treats every fact as equally important and loses the sense of what matters most.

grammar_questions.question:
Read these sentences.

(1) The city plans to extend the Red Line subway to the eastern suburbs. (2) The extended Red Line will serve as a major commuter route for thousands of new residents.

What is the best way to combine the sentences to clarify the relationship between the ideas?

options.A: The city plans to extend the Red Line subway to the eastern suburbs, but this new route will serve as a major commuter route for thousands of new residents.
options.B: The city plans to extend the Red Line subway to the eastern suburbs; afterward, this new route will serve as a major commuter route for thousands of new residents.
options.C: Intending to serve as a major commuter route for thousands of new residents, the eastern suburbs will be reached by an extension of the Red Line subway built by the city.
options.D: Although the city plans to extend the Red Line subway to the eastern suburbs, this new route will serve as a major commuter route for thousands of new residents.

solution.exhibit_text:
(B) adds a semicolon joining two independent clauses plus the logical transition “afterward.” (A) wrongly suggests contrast with “but.” (C) has a misplaced modifier — “Intending to serve...” should modify the extension/route, not “the eastern suburbs.” (D) wrongly suggests contrast with “although.”

**The concept:** When you combine sentences using a connecting word — because, although, while, which, and, but, since — that word has to accurately describe how the two ideas really relate: does one cause the other? Contradict it? Just add detail? Work out the real relationship in plain language first, then check that each answer choice's connecting word actually matches it. A word like "although" promises a contradiction; if the ideas don't actually conflict, "although" is wrong no matter how smooth the sentence sounds.

grammar_questions.question:
(1) Both French croissants and Danish pastries are beloved treats of European baking, but they differ in lamination, shape, and filling. (2) French croissants are often made by folding butter into dough dozens of times, a technique called lamination, before baking it, resulting in a flaky, airy texture that is much lighter and crispier than that of typical Danish pastries. (3) The preparation of Danish pastries involves a sweet glaze, and marzipan, which is folded into the dough before baking. (4) Croissants are traditionally shaped into crescents; Danish pastries, however, are shaped into spirals or pinwheels, which give them a distinctive look and set them apart visually.

Which pair of revisions need to be made in this paragraph?

options.A: Sentence 1: Delete the comma after **baking** AND change **they differ** to **it differs**.
options.B: Sentence 2: Delete the comma after **lamination** AND change **is** to **are**.
options.C: Sentence 3: Delete the comma after **glaze** AND change **is** to **are**.
options.D: Sentence 4: Delete the semicolon after **crescents** AND change **give** to **gives**.

solution.exhibit_text:
In sentence 3, the comma after “glaze” wrongly separates the two ingredients (“a sweet glaze and marzipan”), and “is” should be the plural “are” to match that two-item subject.

**The concept:** A comma goes before "and" when it separates the last item in a list of three or more, or when "and" is joining two complete, independent sentences. But when "and" is just linking two verbs or phrases that share the same subject, no comma belongs before it — adding one wrongly suggests a third list item, or a second full sentence, that isn't actually there.

**The concept:** Subject-verb agreement means the verb has to match whether its subject is singular or plural ("the museum becomes," not "the museum become"). Pronoun agreement works the same way — a pronoun has to match the number of the noun it refers back to. These two rules often get tested together in the same sentence, so check both the verb and any pronouns against their subject/antecedent, not just one or the other.
